notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg3118.tlg002.1st1K-gr: The text opens acephalous, mid-story. Line 1.1: κατήδοντα is evidently corrupt; translated as if κατήσθιον ('they ate up'). κένδυνον read as κίνδυνον, ζωήμ as ζωήν, αἴτησοι as αἴτησαι. The bracketed phrase in 3.1 ('do not be troubled about this') is bracketed by the edition, apparently as a doublet; round-bracketed supplements of the edition are given in square brackets. σπεκουλάτωρ is Latin speculator, an executioner/guardsman.
Line 4.1: φιμιναλίου is taken as Latin feminalia (breeches, drawers). Line 5.1: a stray marginal mark ('ν 80', a page number) in the printed text has been left out.

λοῦπος: a bird (it swoops down carrying a snake), apparently from Latin lupus; species uncertain, so kept untranslated. ἑπτὰ in the first line is an editorial supplement, as is οὐδὲν in the second. Scanning errors read as αἴτιον (σἴτιον), ἑστίασιν (ἑστέασιν), ξύλου (εύλου).

In 10.1 the phrase rendered "seeks your own [ruin]" (σεαυτὸν ἐπιζητεῖ) is obscure and may be corrupt. In 11.1, ποιῆσοι is read as ποιῆσαι. The bracketed [πρὸς αὐτὸν] in 11.1 is the editor's deletion and is not translated.

The bracketed words ', namely a full dish' in the first line are marked by the editor as suspect (probably a gloss); translated in brackets. Round-bracketed (τῇ πόλει) and (πεισθῆναι) are editorial supplements; the latter fits the sentence awkwardly. Scanning errors read as: ἐξῄει, ὁρῶ, κἀγὼ, ἱκανοί; δυνάμεις taken as 'would you have been able' (ἐδύνασο or similar). πίναξ rendered 'dish' (plate or tray). μῖμος rendered 'trickster': literally 'mime', here a rogue or impostor. In the trickster's demand, 'or you redeem [it] with your whole property' renders ἀναρρύσῃ, whose object is unexpressed.

τώτε ὦτε read as τά τε ὦτα ('the ears'); χάρτας read as χάριτας ('thanks'). The phrase rendered 'to apply my hands to punctuating' (πρὸς διάστιξιν (μεμαθηκὼς) συλλαβεῖν) is obscure and the editor's supplement uncertain; διάστιξις may mean writing or marking out text. 'Sponge for a mill workshop' (σπόγγον μυλικοῦ ἐργαστηρίου): presumably a duster for flour; sense uncertain.

Line 3: θέῳ read as θέᾳ ('at the sight of him'); σεριχρίσας read as περιχρίσας, κατα γλαΐσας as καταγλαΐσας. The edition brackets τῆς ἐκεῖθεν ἀπολήψεως, apparently as suspect; translated in brackets. Words in parentheses are editorial supplements, translated. In lines 1 and 2 an article (ὁ) appears to have dropped out before μὲν εἷς and δὲ τοιαύτης.

Words in round brackets (θάνατος, τὸν θεόν, ἂν, ἡ) are editorial supplements in the printed text and are rendered as such. The scripture quotation combines Proverbs 9:8–9 and 23:9, translated as given. 'ὁ τῶν ἀγαθῶν ἔργων': the scanned 'οὐτῶν' read as 'αὐτῶν', 'ἔχ' as 'ἔχῃ', 'ἀλλ μὴν' as 'ἀλλὰ μήν', 'πλέα' taken with 'τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ' though the syntax is awkward. 'ὀφθαλμοῦ δὲ λύχνος' echoes Matthew 6:22.

nodes.text: Of the Narrative of Syntipas
the second recension, as it survives in Munich codex 525, fols. 51–66.

. . . So he says to his mate: "What is this that I have now seen? Did I not order you not to touch these provisions of ours at all?" And his mate answered: "I did not touch them." But he did not believe her at all; instead, growing even more savage against her, he struck her violently and tore her from life, and was left all alone. But when winter came on, and many rains and snowfalls came down, that grain, moistened again by the dampness of the air, filled that whole hole as before. When the dove saw this, he recognised for himself the cause both of the shortfall and of the later refilling to its former level. And from then on he bitterly repented the loss of his mate, but gained nothing from his repentance. So I know, O king, that if you too do away with your son on the mere slander of this accursed woman, and that without knowing anything of the kind about him, the same will happen to your majesty as to the dove I have spoken of: you will be grievously pricked by the goads of repentance, but it will be of no benefit to you. Hear another story of mine too, O king, which shows you the villainies of women. There was a man who practised the art of farming. One day he went out to his field to sow it. Around the hour of the midday meal the farmer's wife prepared dishes of chicken and a honey-cake. She put these in a basket and was carrying them to her husband. It happened that on her way she passed by an inn. As she came along, some highway robbers rushed out from somewhere, seized her, brought her into that inn, and lay with her by force; and taking the dishes she was carrying, they ate them up. Afterwards they left a little of the honey-cake, shaped this remnant into the form of an elephant, and put it back in the basket, without the woman knowing anything about it, and they covered the basket. The woman picked it up, covered as before, and not knowing that the food in it had been eaten by them, set the basket down before her husband's eyes and stepped a little apart. Her husband uncovered it and saw that the basket held nothing else but only the honey-cake that had the shape of the elephant. On seeing this he said to his wife: "What is this, woman?" She, casting her eyes on what she saw, at once contrived to hide the affair that had befallen her. And she says to her husband: "Last night, as I slept, a strange dream appeared to me. I dreamed in my sleep that I was riding on an elephant, and that I slipped off it and was trampled by its feet. When I woke I was gripped by great fear, and at once hurried off with all speed to the dream-interpreter and told him what I had seen; and he, having explained the dream, instructed me, saying: 'You must, woman, make the shape of an elephant out of honey-cake and take it to your husband to eat, so that this dream may be resolved for you without danger.' And now, as you see, I have done this for you according to these instructions; so now, husband, eat it most eagerly, so that no danger may come upon me." And he at once ate the honey-cake. And the woman, having made such an excuse to him without arousing suspicion, escaped the danger from her husband and kept herself thoroughly safe. For her husband believed without question everything she had told him about it. So, O king, recognise for yourself too the intricacy of women's contrivances, and that whatever they wish, they are clever at working mischief and plotting it." And Cyrus, having heard these words in turn, ordered that his son not be put to death.

On the sixth day the woman, greatly vexed and aggrieved at this order of the king, said thus to herself: "If the king's son is not put to death today, tomorrow he will certainly speak to his own father, and at once, through his conversation with him, my mischief will be made plain, and I will be handed over to death. So I must do away with myself; for I will not dare to report anything else to the king." That ill-natured woman, having reasoned this out to herself and being seized with great fear, first gathered her possessions and divided them among her acquaintances and neighbours. Then she asked them to gather fuel for burning for her, and they gathered it in abundance. And she herself kindled a fierce pyre; and when it had been lit, the woman made to throw herself into the furnace, because she suspected that on the morrow she would bring upon herself no small shame and ridicule. Since meanwhile the seventh day too had arrived, on which the boy was to speak to the king, his father, as he had been instructed at the beginning by his teacher, this woman was, as was to be expected, in great anguish and anxiety, and her heart was beset with cares and pains. For she knew that when the boy spoke to the king, she would not only be put to shame, but would also be handed over to destruction along with the shame, for the things she had said so improperly to the boy. Now as this grievous plan of hers was noised abroad in many places and spread by rumour, it reached the ears of the king himself. And indeed he quickly came to the woman ahead of time and says to her: "For what reason, woman, are you giving yourself up to the fire?" She said: "Because you have not avenged me on your son as you should, nor killed him as was fitting." And the king, as soon as she said it, gave her firm sworn pledges that he would without question do away with the boy. She accepted his word and held herself back from this undertaking. And at once the king declared in anger that his son be put to the sword without delay. When this most reckless sentence had been pronounced, the king's most philosophical seventh counsellor, having heard of it, and with him the other six fellow philosophers, were greatly grieved over the offspring of the purple and pained in their souls, seeing the guiltless in danger as a criminal. And they went and came upon the king's *spekoulatôr* [executioner], who was already raising his sword to slay the boy, persistently begging him to put off the boy's execution a little, until the seventh of the philosophers had gone in to the king and come out again. Moreover, they also won the man over with gifts. He, out of respect for the philosophers, assented to their request. Then the seventh of the philosophers, the counsellor, went from there to the king; and on entering he prostrated himself before him on the ground and says: "O king, live! I implore your majesty to recognise that you are attempting to commit a monstrous and at the same time unholy deed, in that you have ordered your son to become the work of the sword, carried away so without examination by a woman's mere suggestion, and that without yet knowing whether she has told you the truth or lies. I have also heard this, that it was through many prayers, fasts and good works that you and his mother obtained this boy from God; and for a woman's word you are handing him over to destruction? But nevertheless, hear my words.

There was a man who had a spirit of divination, and who prophesied the future to those who wished it and earned abundant profit; moreover, along with divination he was also skilled in the art of medicine. Hence he gave ready answers to all who enquired of him about hidden matters. So the man, being thus knowledgeable, amassed no little wealth. Then one day the prophetic spirit that dwelt in him said to the man: "From now on I wish to withdraw from you, and you will have me no longer. But before my departure I will appoint three sayings for you, and with each of them, whatever you ask of God will be granted you on the spot." And having said this, the spirit made known the three sayings to the man. Then it went far away, and that man, the spirit having departed, came home in great despondency. And his wife, seeing him in this state, said: "Why have you come back so gloomy and pale?" He answered her: "Because, woman, that spirit of divination that dwelt in me, through which I prophesied and healed diseases, has now gone out of me and departed entirely. And bereft of it, know that I renounce life itself. For by it I was initiated into every secret and earned abundant profit." When the woman heard this from her husband, she too was greatly pained at what had happened. Seeing her more bitterly distressed, he tried to comfort his wife as best he could, and said to her: "Take heart, woman, and do not grieve; for that spirit appointed three sayings for me, so that through each of them I may ask from God anything that pleases me. And it showed me that whatever I ask will [at once] be done for me by God." At these words the woman became more cheerful and said to her husband: "These three little sayings are enough for you from now on." And the husband replied in turn to his wife: "So what, by God, do you advise me to ask for now?" She, being utterly wicked, given over to disorderly impulses and unreasonable desires, and fond of the body, says: "You know, husband, as I myself also know, that nothing is dearer to people than intercourse; [so] ask the deity that many phalluses grow on your body." And that empty-headed man at once put forward this request, and immediately his own body became covered [and full of phalluses]. Seeing them, the wretch bitterly loathed himself, and struck and abused his wife violently, and grew so savage against her in his anger that he even resolved to kill her without mercy. And he said to her: "Is this your helpful advice, accursed woman? Were you not ashamed to suggest to me a wicked plan for such disgrace?" She replied to him: "Why are you so angry? Have no worry about this; [do not be troubled about this;] for you have two more sayings left. So ask the deity through one saying that these phalluses vanish from you." He, persuaded by his wife, asked this of God, and at once was rid of those phalluses, but along with them he also lost the genitals he had been born with. So again he raged against his wife still more and tried by every means to kill her. But the woman said: "Why are you so eager to kill me? Do not be distressed at this either. For you have one saying left. So ask the deity to get back your natural genitals." He did so, and barely obtained what he asked. See then, O king, what befell that man because the fool thoughtlessly agreed to the woman's most evil counsel. And now, I beg you, be patient, and do not hurry towards the unjust execution of your son, nor be carried away so without examination by the mischief of a wicked woman, especially when the accuser is very clever and ill-natured. But hear another story too.

There was a man who set himself a limit under oath: not to rest at all or give himself any respite, and not to take a wife either, until he had come to know all the contrivances of women. And at once he left his homeland and went round the countries to accomplish what he was so eager for. On the road another man met him, and when he learned from him the urgent need, he says to the man: "You will not be able, fellow, to understand the ways of women or find their end, until you gather ashes, sprinkle some place with them, and spend forty days and forty nights sitting on them, taking only moderate food and drink. For in this way you will be able to count up and mark down the villainies of women." Having heard these words from the man who met him, he did as this man had instructed him, and he went on sitting on ashes, keeping a meagre diet, and for the whole forty days and forty nights writing down the trickeries of women; and in the end he thought these had been completed and that he had left none of them unwritten. So taking the writings he had made, he set off back to his own house. As he went, he came to a certain village, and there he lodged. There was a man in this village who had prepared a feast and invited the inhabitants of the village; along with them he also invited that writer to be entertained. He came and reclined with the other guests, but he did not eat of what was set before them as they did; he sat without eating. So the host says to him: 'Where are you from and who are you, friend?' He answered: 'I am a traveller, as you see, and I come from a distant country. For I left the land that bore me to learn wisdom and to understand the contrivances of wicked women.' When he had said this, the host says to his wife: 'This man is a stranger to this village and has eaten nothing at all. He left his own homeland and has gone round the countries and, as he says, has thoroughly learned all the trickeries of women and set them down in writing. So get up, wife, and prepare for him what is fitting for him to eat and drink, so that he may be properly welcomed by us.' Having said this, the husband goes out. Then the woman, [questioning] the traveller, says: 'What have you done, fellow? Have you written down all the wickedness of women?' And he says: 'Yes, I have written down all their trickeries, and I have set out in detail their deceits and mischiefs, leaving none of them at all unrecorded.' When she heard this from him, she realised that the traveller was empty-headed and senseless. And she said to him in mockery: 'And since, as you claim, you have written down women's contrivances, is it impossible for a woman, even for me myself, to devise something against you, either by word or by some deed? But listen to my words. Look, you see how my husband has come to deep old age, while I am a young woman and very much desire intercourse with men. And you, as I see, are young; and it happens that you have eaten and drunk your fill, and it happens likewise that my husband is away. So get up and fulfil my desire.' When the woman had said this to deceive the traveller, he is persuaded by her words. And getting up, simple-minded and truly foolish as he was, he began to undo the belt of his breeches in order to get onto the bed. But the woman, seeing how quick and ready he was for intercourse, put her hands on her head and shrieked loudly. At once the inhabitants of the village came running to the house at her shriek to see what this was. And the traveller, with her shouting like this, and the villagers coming to her, and the table still standing before him, was terribly frightened, blushing and at a loss at this. The country folk came in and say to the woman: 'Why, woman, did you cry out so loudly?' She says to them: 'This stranger, while being entertained by us and eating from this table, got his throat badly blocked by some morsel and very nearly choked. At once, at this accident, I was suddenly struck with acute distress, and supposing the man was completely dying, I shrieked like this. But now, since God's help came in time, he has been freed from this choking and is back in his former good health.' When she had said this, all those who had run in go out. Then the woman came up to the traveller and spoke thus: 'Will you add to the rest what I have just done to you?' And the stranger says: 'No, not at all.' And she: 'Then in vain, fellow, have you spent your labours and your expense. For after much struggling you attempted what cannot be achieved, and you have not yet understood the trickeries of women.' At these words he roused himself, brought out his writings, and reduced them to ashes in the fire. And then, as if inspired, he said that no mortal could discern the villainies of women. After this, being at a loss and no longer setting himself to investigate women's ways, he returns to his own homeland, and with an untroubled mind took himself a lawful wife.

From these things, then, O king, now related to your majesty by my humble self, know for certain that the wickedness of women is boundless. And do not be carried away so thoughtlessly into doing away with your son on the mere suggestions of so [ill-natured] a woman. For if you put your son to death, who henceforth will trust in your affection?" Cyrus, having listened to these things from the seventh counsellor, the wisest, at once summoned one of his bodyguards, sending him to the *spekoulatôr* [executioner] and ordering that he by no means kill his son. Then, when the eighth day arrived, the boy's tongue was loosed from the bond of silence, and beginning to speak he says to a girl standing before his eyes: 'Go quickly, young woman, and call me the foremost of the philosophers of my father the king.' She, gladly hearing the young man's voice, goes to the philosopher who was most distinguished of the others and reports to him, saying: 'The king's son has begun to speak and summons you to come to him.' At once he came running to him, and embracing him most warmly greeted him. Then the boy, speaking to the philosopher, reveals to him why he had remained silent through the whole seven days; and moreover he made clear to the philosopher everything that the wicked concubine of the king had foolishly said to him. And he added, saying: 'I owe great thanks to God and to you, because you rescued me, the innocent, from a violent and unjust death, and snatched my father the king from the mischiefs of the wicked [woman]. But, my lord, go to the king for me and make known to him all I have shown and told you, before the ill-natured woman goes in to him and corrupts his ears as before.' The philosopher answered the boy: 'Know, young man, that your teacher too, as soon as he hears of your speaking, will come to the king.' And the boy says: 'You have said this truly, my lord; for he too will come to the king today.' When the two had thus spoken with each other, the philosopher rises in haste and goes to the king. And going in to him and paying him the customary prostration, he says to him: 'O king, live for ever! I bring you good tidings of joy: for today your son has been loosed from the bonds of silence and has begun to speak, and he has sent me to your majesty to make known to your royal power everything about him.' And having said this he explained to him everything he had heard from the boy. The king, filled with the greatest joy at the philosopher's message and becoming, as it were, another man from delight, first rewarded the man with gifts for his good news, and then sent some of his bodyguards, summoning the boy with all speed. He quickly came to the king and on entering prostrated himself before him. The king rose from his throne in great joy and graciously went to meet his son, and embracing him greeted him most lovingly. The boy, opening his mouth, wished the king joy. The king, taking him by the hand, bade him sit with him on the royal seat. Then he says to his dearest son: 'What then was the reason, my most beloved child, for such great silence and speechlessness of yours during the past seven days, and why did you not speak to me at all in them, so that through your silence I too was carried away by the woman's words to your destruction and tried to kill you?' The young man answered the king his father: 'God, O king, who is the helper of the human race, he preserved me from slaughter. As for my not speaking to your majesty through the whole past seven days, know, my lord, that I had been instructed by my teacher Syntipas not to utter any word at all within the seven days. And since this woman urged your majesty to my slaughter, I make known to you, O king, about her too: when I came to you after the end of my instruction by my tutor, and shortly afterwards you handed me over to this woman, and she took me off to her house, at once the woman, being wanton, incited me to intercourse with her and wanted me to lie with her. But I, being, as was right, extremely angered at the outrageousness of the thing and most sharply enraged against her, through the confusion and agitation of anger that then possessed me forgot my teacher's command, by which he had enjoined me to keep silent for the seven days. And I answered and said to the woman: "For the present, woman, I will say nothing in reply to you about what you have said to me, until seven days from now have passed; but when they have gone by, I will answer you as is fitting concerning what you have said to me." These words alone, then, O king, did I say in reply to the woman at that time, adding nothing further and saying nothing else until this very day. But because I did not at all then do what pleased the woman, she, seized at once by great fear and suspecting that she would be in danger on my account, hastened to make me a casualty of destruction within the seven days, and the ill-natured woman urged you, O king, to my slaughter. But the reason for my silence has now been made clear to your royal power; for the rest, if it please and be the will of your majesty, let it order a sizeable crowd to assemble and all the philosophers, so that in their hearing, on your royal tribunal, I may reveal the teaching which the philosopher Syntipas taught me.'

When the king heard these words from his son, he rejoiced all the more and exulted greatly. And he orders all the philosophers and men of learning to be gathered together, and his grandees as well. And indeed they all came together in one place to the king. The boy's teacher also arrives, and on entering he prostrated himself on the ground before the king. The king answered and said to him: 'Where have you been until now, most wise Syntipas? For because of your absence I very nearly killed my son.' And Syntipas answered him: 'I, O king, ordered your son to keep silent for [seven] whole days, because, having searched out his fortune by astrological inquiry, I learned that if he spoke within the seven days he would be put to death at once; for this reason I also kept myself far from your majesty until the appointed term of the seven days was completed. And your son did well in not speaking to you at all during them.' The king said: 'The greatest thanks, then, to the immortal God, because he preserved my son from slaughter. For if it had come about that he was put to death by me, my name would have been in danger of being taken from the earth.' Having said this, the king summons the philosophers, and having set them nearer, together with Syntipas, while the boy was seated at the king's right hand as his assessor, he questioned the philosophers, saying: 'Tell me now: if I had killed my son within the seven days, to whom would the blame for his slaughter have been ascribed, to me, to my son, or to the woman?' Four of the philosophers approach the king. One of them answered and said: 'The blame, O king, would have been Syntipas'. For since he knew that your son's speaking within the seven days would bring danger upon him, why did he not keep him with himself, instead of sending him to your majesty?' When the first philosopher had spoken thus, the second answered: 'What you say is not fitting; for no blame attaches to Syntipas, since he was not able to fall short of or exceed the term he had promised the king, nor to deceive the king at all. And for this reason he removed himself far from his eyes and hid, and sent the boy to the king. Hence the blame attaches to the one who ordered the boy's execution.' The third philosopher also answered and said: 'It is not as you say; for the king is not responsible for the matter. But just as nothing is colder than camphor and the wood which custom calls sandalwood, and yet when both are rubbed against each other by someone they produce sparks of fire instead, so too every man, however very intelligent and quick-witted he may be, as soon as he converses with a woman, and especially one he desires, is at once drawn away by her from his own purpose to her will. The woman, then, is to blame for this matter, because by falsely accusing the boy she urged the king to his destruction.' The fourth philosopher came forward and said: 'Nor is it as has been said. For the woman is not to blame either, since the sight of a handsome young man is usually wont to charm a woman's nature, and to ensnare it the more as being softer, if they happened also to converse with each other alone. For then the woman is all the more tickled toward union with the young man and provokes him to the fulfilment of her own desire. Hence this woman too was seized by the same passion; but since the king's son did not consent to her at all, but rather seemed to threaten her, the woman feared him greatly and hastened to protect herself from the danger she suspected. And from this she contrived the young man's death as being to her advantage. Hence the blame attaches to the young man, because he did not keep his teacher's command, but spoke a frightening and harsh word to the woman.' Syntipas also took up [the word] and says: 'It is not as you say; nor is the boy to blame. For nothing is greater than the truth, and everyone who claims to be wise and yet lies to the utmost, all his understanding is brought to nothing; and such a man is not wise, nor is he counted among the company of the wise, but belongs to the assembly of liars and hypocrites.'

The king's son also took up [the word] and says to his father: 'Lord king, permit me too to say something in reply to this.' And the king ordered his son also to answer. And he at once says to the philosophers: 'My knowledge compared to your wisdom is as a fly to a dragon; but nevertheless hear my words. There was a man who, having prepared a costly feast, invited many guests to his hospitality. Then, when they had reclined and were eating, he arranged for them to drink milk. So he sent his slave-girl to the market to buy milk for the invited men. She took the pot, went to the market and bought milk, and putting the pot on her head she was returning to her master's house. As she went, a *loupos* [a bird of prey], swooping down from above and carrying a snake, dropped the snake's venom onto the pot. For the snake, gripped hard by the *loupos*'s talons, spewed out its venom from the great force beside the mouth of the pot. When the venom had been spewed into the milk, the slave-girl noticed [nothing] of this at all. So when this milk was brought into the house, the guests drank it up, and at once they all died. Tell me then, philosophers, who was to blame for the killing?' One of the philosophers took up [the word] and said: 'The host; for he ought not to have given the guests the milk to drink until he had had the slave-girl taste this milk, and only then shared it with his friends.' Another of these philosophers answered and said: 'The matter is not so; for the host is not to blame, but the blame attaches to the snake.' Another took up [the word] and says: 'Nor is it as you say; for the snake does not deserve reproach either, since it spewed out its venom from the force of the grip pressing it, by which it was being forced to choke.' Then another of the philosophers answered: 'The blame rather attaches to the *loupos*, because, as it held and throttled the snake mightily, the snake was driven to spew.' Syntipas too came forward and says: 'Let it be known to you, men, that every living creature made by God that has vital power eats nothing other than what God assigned to its nature. Therefore the *loupos* too, ordained to be fed on the creeping things of the earth, is blameless in what happened.' When the philosophers had said this, the king gazed at his son and says to him: 'I think, son, that the philosophers present do not know to which of these the blame belonged. But you, tell me who was to blame.' The boy answered the king: 'In no respect, lord king, are the philosophers mistaken, nor do they speak variously as though stumbling against the truth. But the danger that befell those who drank the milk was laid up in their destiny, and they were fated to depart from life in this manner.' The king, accepting the answer as very fitting, was delighted at his son's great understanding and his reasoned and wise reply. And he says to Syntipas: 'Ask whatever you wish and it will be awarded to you by my royal power. But also, if you have any further teaching, teach this too to my son.' Syntipas said to the king: 'Let it be known to your majesty, O king, that I have left out nothing at all of the art of wisdom and eloquence which I have not taught your son, so that he has become superior to all the philosophers under your rule.' The king took up [the word] and said to his grandees and the philosophers under him: 'Is Syntipas telling us this truthfully?' They answered: 'Very much so, lord.' He looked at his son and says: 'And what do you say, child? Does your teacher say this about you in truth?' The philosophers answered in the boy's place and said: 'No one excels in elegance of speech as your son does.' So the boy says to the king: 'I make known to your majesty, lord, that if any man does not have perfect understanding, he does not return good to those who have benefited him; and we know such a man rather to be perverse. But this man, taking careful pains, made me most accomplished in philosophy and knowledge. And he ought to receive from your royal power a reward worthy of his care. And since, O king, these philosophers of yours also bear witness for me that I surpass even them in eloquence, hear the present tale of mine.

For there happened to be two children, one five years old, the other three. And there was also a certain old man, crippled and paralysed as well, who together with them was adorned with understanding and sharpness of mind.
But the king, breaking off the thread of the story, says to his son: 'And what, child, was their story?' The boy, taking up the account from the beginning, told it, saying:

'There was a certain lecherous man. Whenever he heard of a good-looking woman, he would go to her at once for the sake of debauchery. So one day he was told of a certain very beautiful woman, and he went off to her at once for the sake of intercourse. That woman had a child who happened to be three years old in age. At that moment he happened to say to his mother: "Prepare me something to eat, mother." She, seeing that man pressing for debauchery with her, says to him: "Wait a little for me, sir, until I prepare something to eat for my child." He took up [the word] and said to the woman: "Leave the care of the child for now and carry out this business of ours, lest I happen to be delayed here." She answered the man: "If you knew, sir, what sharpness of mind this child of mine possesses, you would not say such things to me." And having said this she gets up at once, and having cooked what food there was, which happened to be rice, she set it before the child. He, although he was not wholly an infant in age, nevertheless kept on wailing and forced his mother to set more rice before him: "For I am not yet full," he says, "but I want more." The mother did as the child wished; but he again, wanting yet another helping, lamented to his mother all the more. That licentious man, however, annoyed at the child's wantonness and his unceasing crying, says to him: "Truly you are very shameless and insatiable, and there is no sense in you at all, as I see. For if such food had been set before five men, it would have amply sufficed them to the full." The boy took up [the word] and said: "It is rather you who are deprived of all sense, since what you are now seeking and saying indecently to my mother seeks your own [ruin], and you pursue a deed hated by God. But what do you see in me that is deprived of sense? Indeed, from this crying of mine, which you call shamelessness, what harm at all do I suffer? Rather, my eyes, cleansed by the tears, have become brighter, and my nostrils have been wiped clean of the impurity in them, and the food set before me has been added to me, and through this very crying whatever I wanted came to me easily." Hearing these sensible words, that man understood that this child surpassed him in sense. And he got up and, holding both his hands in a gesture [of respect], bowed down to the child and says: "Do not blame me, I beg, for what I said to you. For I did not know that you possessed such sense." And having said this, he immediately withdrew from there, having done nothing improper to his mother.

Hear then, lord king, the tale about the five-year-old child as well. There were three men, who were partners with one another. They set out for trade to a distant country. Holding to their journey, they enter a certain village and took lodging with an old woman. After this they decided to go off to the bath-house and wash. And they say to the old woman: "Get ready for us, woman, the necessary things and wraps." She got everything ready for them, but forgot only the comb. They took out the three purses of gold they were carrying, in which they had their common treasure, handed them to the old woman, and ordered her to keep them with her: "And do not give any of them to anyone until you see the three of us come to you together." Having instructed the old woman so, they went off to the bath-house. And having gone in, since they saw they had no comb, they send one of them to the old woman to fetch the comb. The one sent said to her: "My partners make known to you through me, woman: send us the gold we deposited with you." She says to him: "I will by no means give you anything until the three of you are together." He says to her: "Look, my partners are standing in your sight, as you see, and are calling to you from afar to give me this gold." Having said this he calls to them about the comb, speaking without naming it and unclearly, thus: "The old woman gives me nothing unless you permit her." They called to her, saying: "Give [it] to him, woman." She took out the gold deposited with her and handed it to him. He, having taken it, at once ran away from there. His partners went on waiting for him a long time; then they call to the old woman: "Where is that partner of ours who was sent to you, since he has not appeared to us at all?" The old woman said to the men: "He asked me for your treasure, and in accordance with your calling out and urging I handed it over to him. And having taken it he left my house." They replied to the woman: "We sent him to you in front of us to ask for the comb." The old woman says: "But he asked me for your gold as at your urging. And I, urged by you, as he called out, to give [it] to him, took it out, as you said, and handed it over to him." The merchants, having heard this unexpectedly from the woman and seized bitterly by heavy despondency, snatched her up together and go to the ruler of the country and recount the affair to him with great feeling. The ruler said to the woman: "Give back to them the gold deposited with you by them." The old woman answered him: "I, my lord, gave back to them their treasure." The merchants countered her objection: "We, judge, being three partners, when we deposited our money with the old woman, at once gave her instructions with every safeguard, saying: 'By no means, woman, let this deposit of ours leave your hands, unless you see the three of us together seeking to receive it from you.'" The ruler again said to the old woman: "Give back the gold to the merchants, woman, and dispute no further about these things." The old woman goes out from the ruler's presence lamenting bitterly and crying out mournfully. A little later a certain child, who was five years old, meeting her as she lamented, and pitying her for her bitter wailing, said to the woman: "Why do you lament so piteously, woman?" She said to the child: "Let me, child, wretched as I am, bewail my misfortune." But he kept pressing her hard, asking the cause of her lamenting, and did not leave her until the woman had explained everything to him. He replied to her: "I will free you now from the misfortune that holds you. But if you want me to do this, first give me one silver coin, so that with it I may buy myself nuts." The woman says: "If you free me from this grievous distress, I will give you the silver coin." The boy says to her: "Go back then to the ruler and speak to him thus: 'I make known to you, my lord, that there were three partners who deposited this gold with me, as indeed was made known to your highness before. They also instructed me, saying: "See that you do not give the money deposited with you to any one of us, unless the three of us come to you together." Now, my lord, see, the gold is with me; order then the three partners to present themselves to me together, just as, as I said, they themselves bound me with exactness. And so their common treasure will be given back to them by me.'" Greatly delighted, then, by these persuasive suggestions of that child, the woman quickly returns to the governor and spoke to him what the child had set out, as clear and sensible. The governor, recognising that the woman spoke reasonably, summons the merchants and says to them: "This woman now speaks reasonably to us; so present to her, together with yourselves, your other partner too, just as you yourselves instructed her. Then in this way the three of you together will receive back the gold." When such a verdict had been delivered by the judge, and the woman was no longer dragged about by those two men, the ruler understood that the accused old woman had been taught this last defence by someone else. And summoning her he asked her who had suggested this persuasive counter-argument to her. She answered: "A five-year-old child met me and, seeing me lamenting, pitied me and pointed out this counter-argument." The governor at once sent for the child, and when he came questioned him, saying to him: "Did you, child, truly suggest this argument to the old woman?" He says: "Yes, my lord." The judge, astonished at the child's understanding and sharpness of mind, at once appoints him teacher of rhetoricians and philosophers.

"Hear also, my lord king, the story of the old man. There was a man who was accustomed to trade, and he bought aromatic woods for trading. Having learned of a certain city that there was a scarcity of such things there, he quickly took what he had bought and drove to that city. When he came near it he made his lodging outside, having chosen first to learn from there how the sale of these woods stood in that city. Meanwhile a woman, who happened to be the slave of one of the men in the city, saw the merchant and said to him: 'Where are you from, friend? And what is it you are bringing?' The merchant answered: 'What I am bringing is aromatic woods.' She went in to her own master and made clear to him everything about that merchant. He, being wily and crafty in character, at once gathered the aromatic woods he had at his own house, which were few, and threw them on the fire. And when he blew on it a great fragrance went out from there. The merchant outside smelled it and says to those with him: 'I smell a great aromatic fragrance. So look quickly and very carefully whether some fire has come near any of our loads, and our spices are burning.' They say: 'Not at all; no fire or spark whatever has touched any of our loads.' When morning came the merchant enters the city, and as he drives in the master of that slave woman meets him. Then he asks him what it is that he has in his cargo. The merchant says: 'I have brought aromatic woods for sale to whichever of the inhabitants of this city want them.' He again [said]: 'Who forced you, man, to bring these to this city, and to pass over the other kinds of goods which would have been profitable to you? For know for certain that the people here use such woods as a kind of firewood, and employ them for heating the furnace.' 'But I,' says the merchant, 'heard that this city above all cities was most in need of and short of such things.' He [said] to him: 'Those who told you this deceived you greatly.' Stricken at heart by these words, the merchant was overcome with grief. That man, seeing him overcome with distress, said to him: 'I see, friend, that you have become terribly grieved, and I pity you for your deep dejection. Come now, sell me your whole cargo, and whatever you want I will give you, a full dish.' The merchant, reasoning with himself, said: 'It is better for me, as I reckon, to take whatever this man gives me than to have my whole merchandise left unsold.' And having thought this, he sold him his entire cargo, having agreed about the price he was to receive [, namely a full dish]. So the man took what he had bought and carried it to his own house. The merchant, however, going through the city, lodged with his partners at the house of an old woman. And he asked her, saying: 'How, woman, are the aromatic woods sold in the city?' She said to him: 'For their weight in gold. But, merchant, look, I tell you, be on your guard against the inhabitants of this city. For they are all crafty and wily, and there is no one of those who come here who does not nearly come to ruin at the hands of its citizens.' When the old woman had said this, he went out of her house a little later to see the sights of the city, and he sees three men sitting together. He stood gazing at them intently. And when they had seen this merchant, one of them said: 'Come, father, let you and me debate with each other, and whichever gets the better of the other, let him order the loser to do whatever the winner wishes.' The merchant, following a simple mind and an unsuspecting understanding, says: 'Yes, let it be as you have proposed.' Then they sat debating with each other; and that trickster and crafty man defeated the merchant, and said to him: 'See, as you see, I have got the better of you in argument. Now do what I order you. I want you to drink up the waters of the sea.' At this the merchant, falling into dejection and helplessness, could not put forward any plausible counter-argument to the trickster and escape his snares. Now the merchant was grey-eyed; and it happened that another of the three, a trickster, was one-eyed, and he too had a grey eye. And he got up and seized the merchant forcefully, saying: 'You have stolen my other eye. So let us both go to the ruler of the city, so that through him you may give back to me the eye you have stolen from me.' The old woman who had received the merchant heard this too, and that the trickster was dragging the merchant to the ruler of the land. And meeting them as they went she said to the trickster: 'Leave this man, the merchant, with me for today, I beg, on my surety, and I will present him to you early in the morning.' He yielded to her request and gave her the man. The old woman took him and went back home. And she began to reproach him, saying: 'Did I not warn you beforehand to be on your guard against the citizens of this (city), because they are tricksters, wicked in mind, and wily in every way? And do not go out among them openly at all any more. But since before you did not heed my advice, and so have found the wages of your disobedience, now at least heed me about what I want to put to you. For I inform you that these tricksters have an aged teacher, who in the advantages of wickedness greatly excels and surpasses the others. So all the tricksters every evening resort to him as their teacher and report to him in detail what each has said and done during the whole day. Now then, hear my profitable counsel: get up, change your appearance, and dress and make yourself up as one of those tricksters. Then go secretly and mingle yourself in their gathering. But take care not to be detected by them. Go along with them as far as the teacher, and standing near him unnoticed, like one of the ordinary common men of the city, listen to what those who dealt with you will report to him and what he will answer them. And whatever he says to them, note it in your mind, so that by setting his answers to them against those who are fighting you, you may overcome their craftiness by force; and from this a very great profit will come to you.' The merchant did all that he had been taught by the old woman. And after changing his appearance he stood very close to that old man, and first he saw come to him the man who had bought his aromatic woods. He reported to that teacher, saying: 'I met a merchant bringing some aromatic woods for sale, and bought up his whole cargo, giving him what I agreed, namely a dish filled with whatever goods he might see fit to ask of me.' The teacher answered him, saying: 'And what is it you agreed to give him? Gold? Silver?' The trickster says: 'No, my lord; none of these, but unnamed kinds [of goods], whatever he himself might want, a full dish.' The teacher said to him: 'You have made a great mistake. For if the merchant happened to ask you for fleas, a full dish, half of them to be female and the other half male, and moreover to be grey-blue, would you have been able to give him such a payment? How could you have escaped him?' The trickster says to him: 'This merchant, my lord, is not so clever, nor was his mind capable of such craftiness. But, as I think, he is going to ask me for either gold or silver.' Then the one who had beaten the merchant in debate came forward too and reported, saying: 'I too contended with the merchant in conversation and the weaving of arguments, and having defeated him I ordered him to drink all the waters of the sea. For so it had been agreed between us, that the one beaten in argument should accept and do whatever was ordered by the winner.' The teacher answered him: 'Neither have you acted well. For suppose perhaps he were to reply to you: "Go first and hold back the rivers that flow into the sea; then in this way I will drink the water of the sea, which alone I agreed with you to drink." If then he says this to you, will you easily be able to check the rivers from flowing into the sea?' The trickster says: 'But know that the merchant's sense is not sufficient to make such a reply to me.' Then the one-eyed trickster too came forward and said to the old man: 'I too, my lord, saw in the market a foreign merchant who was grey in the eyes. And seizing him I said to him: "You and I are both grey-[eyed], and you have stolen one of my eyes. So I will by no means let go of you until I take out one of your eyes and fasten it to my forehead, or you redeem [it] with your whole property."' The teacher said: 'Neither have you achieved anything. For if he sees fit to reply to you: "First, to establish this claim of yours, take out this one eye which you have, and I likewise will put out one of my eyes, and let us both weigh them; and if they are found equal in weight to each other, it is clear that my one eye is yours; but if one of the two eyes being weighed appears heavier than the other in the pan of the scale, then my other eye is not yours, but rather you will be duly called to account for putting it out." If then the merchant answers you this, will he not entirely dissuade you from your claim? And the worst of it is that if this happens to you, you will be completely deprived of sight and become entirely eyeless, whereas he, still having one of his eyes afterwards, will go on seeing the light.' To this the one-eyed trickster replies to the teacher: 'But this merchant is not so crafty as to put forward against me such a plausible defence.' While these things were thus being said and answered back between the tricksters and their teacher, the merchant listened very well and secretly through that whole night and kept these things in his own heart. When morning came the man who had bought the aromatic woods comes to the merchant. And the merchant says: 'Give me, friend, whatever you agreed to provide me in return for the cargo sold to you.' The trickster said to him: 'Ask whatever you want, and I will readily provide it to you.' The merchant [said]: 'I want you to give me in the dish as many fleas as it will hold, half of the swarm male and the other half female, and all of them grey-blue in appearance.' Having said this to the trickster, the merchant kept pressing him hard and using much force against him, until the trickster, even against his will, gave him an amount greater than the fair price of his aromatic woods; and so he was rid of his harassment. Meeting also the other two tricksters, the one contending about the eye and the one who had ordered him to drink up the sea, he demanded that they too do what he had secretly heard from their teacher. And he kept throttling them too, until the merchant received from them as many gifts as he wanted (to be persuaded); and so they were rid of his harassment. And now, my lord king, from what I have told you know that both those two children, the three-year-old and the five-year-old, of whom I told you before, and this aged teacher, were adorned with much knowledge and understanding; and like them my teacher too has made me a teacher."

The king replied and said to his son: 'Tell me, child, how in the previous three years you did not learn the eloquence that has now come to you, while now, in only the past six months, you have become so wise?' The boy answered the king: 'At that time, O king, while I was still an infant, the senses of body and soul that I possess did not work together with one another. For then, since my body was entirely immature, neither my eyes nor my tongue nor my heart cooperated with one another toward the learning of instruction. For it is not possible for one who is still childish in mind to be taught knowledge easily, since every child, taking pleasure in games and idleness, does not set his mind attentively on instruction. And I too, O king, being in the same way at that time in both age and understanding, could gain no fruit at all from what I was taught, since I did not fix my mind on these things at all, but, being childish, kept it scattered. But my teacher Syntipas, observing the youthfulness of my age, did not teach me heavily, nor did he use difficult words with me at the beginning, so that I should not be worn down from the start by the weight of difficult and hard-to-grasp things and cast out of my mind everything I was taught — for my teacher knew that if he taught me immoderately from the beginning, I could easily have rebelled against him and left him, since I am a king's son — but by shaping me little by little with his words he thus skilfully led me up to the perfection of philosophy. And I, laying hold of a more mature understanding, kept in my heart all the things taught me by him, and gathering together my formerly scattered reason, straining my ears to listening and my tongue to the practice and weaving of words, and (having learned) to apply my hands to punctuating, I thus in the space of only six months grasped most exactly everything taught me, and came to share in all philosophy and understanding, the divine power surely also helping both me and the zeal of the one who initiated me.' The king, greatly delighted in heart at these words of the boy, sent up words of thanksgiving to God, and kept extolling to the utmost the boy's understanding and philosophy, and acknowledged his thanks to Syntipas. Then he orders that wicked woman, who had plotted to destroy his son, to be brought before him; and when she stood there, the king says to her: 'Reveal to me, woman, holding nothing back out of fear, why you were eager to destroy my son, and what the manner of this mischief of yours was.' The woman replied and said: 'You know, most mighty king, that nothing is dearer to any man than his own life. For even if someone lives in poverty or is oppressed by some misfortune of life, he nonetheless still clings to his own life. Now, I took your boy to myself at your command for this reason: that, out of service to your majesty, I might find out from him in private by what cause he was restrained from speaking. And I kept coaxing him with all sorts of questions and flatteries, and softening the hardness of his silence with gentle words, until I induced him to answer me one word. This he uttered angrily and sharply, and said to me: "I will answer you nothing for now, woman, until seven days from now have passed. Then I will give you the answer you deserve." I, greatly alarmed at this word and becoming very frightened, and suspecting that I would be exposed to danger from the boy, saw how to escape by contrivance the ruin [coming] from him. And thereupon, impelled by satanic working, I lied against your son and treacherously accused him before your majesty. I know my sin and confess it openly, denying nothing of it. But you, most great king, do with me what seems good to you, as your God-guided majesty may please.' The king, looking at his grandees who stood by, says to them: 'What counsel do you give my majesty about this matter, and of what punishment would this woman be worthy?' One of the grandees replied and says to the king: 'It is just, O king, that her hands and feet be cut off.' Another says: 'Justice does not seem so good to me; rather, it is fitting that her heart be dug out while she is alive.' And another of them again said in reply that her tongue should be cut out. The woman, hearing such verdicts and what punishments they were proposing to the king for her, spoke a fable of this sort to them, saying: 'What you declare against me, grandees, is like the example of a certain fox, who used to enter a certain city by night. Her way in was through the window of the little house of a certain leather-worker. And whenever she entered his house through it, she ate up his hides. Then that leather-worker, seeing the tears that had been made in his hides, at once sets a very strong trap for her. The fox afterwards, entering again through that window as was her habit, is at once caught in the trap. But the fox, being wicked and wily, escaped the trap that held her by some well-devised contrivance. And she went round the whole city to find some other window through which she could get out of the city; but it was walled in on every side. And though she toiled the whole night, she could find no way out at all; and as the day was dawning, she reasoned with herself and said: "If day comes on, I shall be seen by the dogs, and they will not leave me alone until they have divided my flesh among them. But I know what I must do." And having said this she goes to the gate of the city, and stretching herself out near the doorpost on the inside, she pretended to be dead and breathless. She used this device waiting for the city gate to be opened, so that she might at once make her escape through it in a rush and be rid of the danger she feared. When she was thus stretched out as if dead, and the gate had been opened toward dawn, someone saw her and said to himself: "Truly the tail of this fox is very useful as a ready sponge for a mill workshop." Saying this, he at once drew his knife and cut it off. The fox, her tail cut off, bore it bravely in silence. Then another man passing by and seeing her spoke thus: "I have heard that if one of the infants goes on crying for a long time, there is nothing else for curing him and stopping his crying like a fox's ears. If these were carried by this child, his crying would not go on long." And having said this he cut off that fox's ears with a knife. And the fox bore this too bravely, (so that) by the (appearance) of being dead she might escape death. Another man passing through there said to the others: "I too, men, have heard that if someone has pain and suffering in his teeth, he should pull out a fox's tooth and put it on the suffering tooth, and at once he will obtain a cure of the affliction." So that man too, having said this, at once took up a stone and smashed all the fox's teeth; and she bravely endured this punishment too. And thus she went on enduring the pains, until another man passing by said: "I too have heard that the fox's heart serves as a pain-relieving drug, and that it is healing for all diseases." So that man too, having said this, at once drew a knife and tried to dig out her heart. At that very hour it happened that the city gate was opened; and at once the fox leapt out and ran off through the gate at great speed and escaped the danger hanging over her. And I too now, wretched as I am, O king, am ready to endure all the other things that the grandees of your majesty have advised your majesty, but to bear having my heart dug out I cannot. For it is the cause of a violent death.'

To this the king's son answered and said to his father and to the grandees standing by: 'The woman speaks truly and fittingly. For it is not right for men who are intelligent and sound of mind to lay blame and accusation on the failings of women. So then, no sentence of punishment and penalty is fitting for this woman either; only this should be done to her: that her head be shaved and her face smeared with soot, and that they hang a bell from her neck; then, having made her ride backwards on a donkey, they should parade her through the whole city, with two heralds running alongside her, one going ahead of her and the other following behind; and they must shout in the hearing of all the outrage that the woman committed.' When the boy had spoken thus, the king was pleased at what was said, and the grandees too bore witness, approving. And the king said to the boy: 'You have spoken excellently, my child, and truly advised us wisely. Let what my son has advised us be done to the woman.' And what the king's son had recommended to his father concerning her was carried out on the wicked and crooked woman.

Then the king said to the philosopher Syntipas: 'Reveal to me, philosopher, and set out clearly, where such great intelligence and philosophy came to my son from: did he have his learning by nature from his very birth, or rather has he been made wise through your care?' Syntipas answered and said to the king: 'Your son's intelligence and knowledge together, O king, were supplied to him from above in the first place; and the very fortune of his birth enriched him with the advantage of knowledge, as you said; and then, through my care and diligence above all, he gained his unrivalled excellence in knowledge. But on this matter, O king, hear a story of mine as well.' The king said: 'Tell it, Syntipas, wisest in counsel.' And he began the following account to him:

'There was a king in very ancient times, who kept a great many philosophers about him. One of them happened to be far more distinguished than the others. That king also had another man, highly trained in the art of star-gazing. Now to that chief philosopher of the king a son was born, and this was announced to the king. The king at once summoned the astrologer; and he, having first learned about the boy born to the philosopher, inquired into his fortune and declared to the king: "This boy, my lord, from what the courses of the stars teach me, has the wickedness of robbers and evildoers; and he will live for many years; but in the thirteenth year of his life he will commit a very great crime and theft." When the astrologer had said this, the father of the newborn said to him: "Have you now truthfully made known to the king all that concerns the fortune of the newborn boy?" He said: "Yes, philosopher; having examined and investigated the boy's affairs precisely, I found that he will be a robber, and of robbers the most dangerous and most destructive." The philosopher answered and said to the king: "Then I will train and educate my boy so that he never conceives any such deed, but rather keeps away from forbidden acts and holds fast to good and praiseworthy ones." Now the boy, when he had passed eight months of age, was at once weaned from his mother's breast. After this his father shut him up inside a small chamber and began to feed and rear him on tender and wholesome foods, and moreover to teach him every virtue and dignity. And so he raised his son with strictness: he allowed no one at all to go in to him, nor the boy to come out of the house, nor was anything of the wicked deeds of human life made known to him at all. And being raised thus, the boy reached the age of fifteen. Then his father said to him: "Tomorrow, my child, I shall go to the king, and I wish to take you with me to him, so that you may greet him and converse with him as is proper, after the customary and servile obeisance." So the philosopher spoke to his son. And he had trained him thoroughly in learning, being eager to show the astrologer's prophecy false. But the boy, hearing that his father wished to bring him in to the king, was rather anxious at what he heard, and turned it over in his mind, saying: "I have never seen the king before, and now my father wishes to bring me in to him. I too must bring him perfumes and aromatic wares and something else, and praise his majesty, as is fitting. But I am ashamed to ask my father for such wares. Still, I know what I must do." The following night he went out secretly from his father's house and went to the king's palace. Then, making a breach in its wall in the manner of thieves, he slipped into the royal quarters as far as the royal bedchamber itself. And at once the king, waking up, suddenly saw him, and was gripped with fear at the sight of him. And greatly alarmed, he said to himself: "Had this man not possessed very great boldness, he would not have dared to come in here at such an untimely hour of the night; and if I try to oppose him, perhaps he will attempt to kill me." So that king, having reasoned thus, kept quiet instead and allowed the young man [to take away from there] whatever wares he might wish to take. He stretched out his hands, touched the royal fabrics lying there, and drew out one of them, a linen cloth of great value. Taking only this, he left the palace and went far off. He sold the cloth at once, and with the price bought myrtle scents and other perfume wares in plenty. The king, however, made the young man's nocturnal visit known to no one at all. At dawn, then, the philosopher took his son and went to the king. And going in, they prostrated themselves on the ground before him. And at once the boy presented to the sovereign those fragrant and most delightful wares he had bought, and by means of this offering began to praise him. And the philosopher said to him: "O king, live for ever. See, as you behold, I have presented this boy of mine to your majesty, whom your astrologer foretold would begin a robber's work at about the thirteenth year of his life. And see, he is now fifteen and has committed no theft whatever. Therefore the astrologer has now been caught out as false, and his predictions have been shown to be nonsense." But the king, gazing intently at the young man's face, recognised him as the thief who had made the breach in the night, boldly slipped into the palace and committed the theft in his bedchamber. And he answered: "This is the thief who broke in against my majesty." And the astrologer's prediction was confirmed all the more in him. From this story of mine, most mighty king, know that at each person's birth a particular outcome of good fortune (or misfortune) is laid up from God. Just as at your son's birth there came to him afterwards what is useful and praiseworthy and full of good fortune, so at the birth of the boy born to the philosopher of that king, of whom I told you, there came what is useless, to be shunned and rejected, and full of misfortune.' When Syntipas had told this to King Cyrus, the king said to his son: 'Tell me, beloved child, how and in what way your instructor Syntipas taught you such great philosophy.' The boy answered his father: 'Since you still seek, my lord, to learn about this, I make known again to your majesty that my teacher, having taken me from you and led me to his house, at once built a new small chamber for me, and having neatly plastered it inside and brightened it with whitewash, he depicted on the walls of the room everything he had to teach me, marked it out in letters and arranged it precisely. Moreover he painted the sun, the moon and the stars on them. And on the same walls he engraved, with ornaments, the ten chapters of wisdom (and) knowledge and teaching. Of these the first chapter introduces a perverse and abusive man, who fans quarrels and fights between two people, whether kinsmen or friends. The second presents a philosophic man, who brings great benefit to his friend. The third introduces a man of crafty mind, who never knows how to grow drowsy in wickedness, stitching together tricks and mischief against another without his knowing. The fourth is about a man who unbecomingly reproaches another for some disfigurement present on his body, perhaps from leprosy, or something else of the kind. The fifth, that one should not pronounce on any matter or accusation before its truth has been confirmed. The sixth chapter, that one should not trust a foolish and ignorant man. The seventh chapter teaches about an envious man, jealous of other men because they enjoy some good or happen to share in some praiseworthy advantage; who, begrudging them, is grieved within himself and wastes away with envy, but in no way harms those he envies by it. The eighth chapter is about how one should love all and never repay like for like to one who has done him harm. The ninth chapter sets out that as one wishes another to do to him, so he should likewise do to that other. And the tenth chapter shows that one should not make friends or sworn brothers with those who are impious and tyrannical in their deeds and practise injustice and greed.'

When the king had heard these things thus from his son, he sent up words of thanksgiving to God, and continued praising Syntipas; and indeed he also honoured the man with lavish gifts. Then he said to the boy as follows: 'Most beloved child, do the things that happen to someone usually happen from fated fortune?' The boy said to the king: 'Many people think that this is so, master; but the cause of the grievous things that happen comes from people's wickedness. For they do not conduct their affairs justly, but crookedly and unjustly. For it is their custom, when they meet one of the philosophers, who advises what is good and needful and profitable, unless such a man is also wealthy and distinguished in honour, rather to despise him and overlook him as an ignorant man and not to count him one of the philosophers; and so they do not incline their ear to his words at all. But if someone is prosperous in life and flourishing and deemed worthy of honour by all, yet is wholly deprived of wisdom and intelligence, people pay more heed to him, even if he is ignorant in mind. People do not do this well, but rather wrongly.' Again then the king asked his son: 'To whom, then, does kingship belong?' The boy said: 'To the intelligent and sensible man, so that the subjects may thereby be well governed, and nothing unjust be allowed to be done by anyone, and the ruler not subject anyone to condemnation before the truth has been lawfully confirmed; and so that he may render good things to the upright and good, and to the perverse and wicked the corresponding pains, and keep the fear of God before his eyes and reckon nothing more precious than justice.' The king again said to his son: 'What kingdom, child, stands most secure?' And the boy said: 'The one that reveres God and pursues justice, which also pities the poor and restores and benefits those of its subjects who are in a bad way and oppressed by the misfortunes of life.' The king said: 'And in what kind of kingdom do people delight?' The boy said: 'In one that has come about by divine providence, and is justly governed, and holds fast to every good work towards those under it.' Again the king inquired of his son: 'Does the wisdom of the philosophers, my child, prevail over the cunning of others?' The son said to the king: 'Knowledge greatly prevails over cunning and can surpass it in all things, since it surely distinguishes the differences between actions and separates what is by nature good from its opposites. For the cunning present in some people does not belong to intelligence and wisdom, but to mere thought and intention and shrewdness.' The king asked again: 'Why do philosophers feel no shame before anyone at all, but boldly put forward their teaching to everyone?' The boy answered and said: 'For this reason, O king, they are shameless: because they long to teach all, and especially the more intelligent and those who aspire to wisdom.'

'Who, then,' said the king, 'are those hated by the philosophers?' The boy answered: 'All who do not receive their teaching with a most upright mind, but bear their rebukes bitterly, as though taking offence at the truth.' And the king said again: 'What treasure is better than the others?' The son answered him: 'That of good works.' The king said: 'What does one need against adversaries?' The boy said: 'Trust in God.' The king said: 'Who is truly the richest?' The boy said: 'He who trusts in the divine and possesses good works.' The king said: 'Who is it that possesses the better rest?' The boy said: 'He who begrudges no one, and blames himself but does not condemn another.' The king said: 'Who is truly a fool?' The boy said: 'He who does not understand his own fault and does not heed the one who advises him well.' The king said: 'Which of men has the best and most friendly disposition?' The boy: 'He who grieves no one at all, and is not jealously disposed towards anyone.' The king said: 'What way of thinking is abominable to God?' His son said: 'That which is arrogant and boastful. And indeed folly and idle chatter of unseemly words are hateful to him.' The king said: 'Which of shameful deeds, full of sin, envelops the one who practises it?' The youth said: 'Envy and false witness, insatiability and greed, and for someone to go after his own desires through neither fearing God nor feeling shame before man; through which he senselessly offends and sins. These are the deeds of a sinful life.' The king said: 'And who is it that does not understand these things?' The youth said: 'He who is insatiable in all things and very fond of money.' The king said: 'Whom should one fear and tremble before?' The boy said: 'The one who does not fear (God) nor judge justly. And indeed one must also dread a treacherous friend and an ill-disposed hypocrite, who utters one thing with his mouth and wickedly devises another in his heart.' The king said: 'Why, then, do people more often make enemies of one another than embrace friendship?' The boy said: 'Because the doing of harm is easy for the doer, while the doing of good is very difficult.' Again the king: 'How is it that the sick man gladly accepts the doctors' orders, even if they seem burdensome, but people, when the truth is spoken to them, bear it grievously?' The son said to the king: 'Because the sick man gladly accepts the medicines given him, even if they are somewhat unpleasant and very bitter, as bringing health and joyful well-being; but the foolish and unintelligent man, when true and needful things are said to him, bears them grievously and is vexed at them, since he is not driven to what is fitting by any force or pain, as the sick man is. For this reason it is also written: Rebuke a wise man and he will love you; give a wise man an occasion and he will be wiser. And do not rebuke a fool, lest he hate you; and do not speak your words into a fool's ears, lest he sneer at them.' And the king said again to his son: 'How is it that the one who eats plentifully is at once sated, but the one who loves money has an insatiable desire for it?' The boy answered: 'A man's belly, which receives the food, after taking it plentifully certainly reaches satiety, even if he does not wish it; but the lamp of the eye, as much as it sees money, so much it desires it and is insatiable towards it, until through death its sight is covered under the dust, as is customary.' Then the king said again: 'What would the death of an envious and begrudging man turn out to be?' And the boy: 'The (death) of such a man becomes a gain for others. For none of the lawless deeds is worse than envy, and every person should earnestly ask the divine that envy be utterly rooted out of his heart. Know, O king, that every person who does not envy eats with great pleasure, drinks with pleasure, and sleeps with pleasure. For his way of life is free of care, his life is set free of pain, (his) sitting is untroubled and his standing without toil. These things, then, most mighty king, which you have heard from me, are sufficient for the best way of life and a blameless life for sensible men like you, and intelligent men, and those who aspire to philosophy.'
